# ML compilers, from zero

> A free, open-source course where you build a machine learning compiler from scratch, in Python or OCaml. It is inspired by the public syllabus of CMU 10-411, Compilers for Machine Learning, and is independent: not affiliated with CMU or George Hotz.

The compiler works on a small graph IR of UOps, written in a text format called .uir. Each week adds ops and a spec, and a test suite grades your compiler against a reference implementation. Week 0 teaches the prerequisites (C, memory and caches, IRs, tensors, matmul, and the language you write the compiler in). Every lesson has quizzes with hints and answers, and graded exercises that run in the browser editor.

Source code, tests and the reference compiler: https://github.com/wilsonmike/ml-compilers-course

## Start here

- [ML compilers, from zero](https://sharpterminal.com/site/): A course where you build a machine learning compiler yourself, one week at a time. You start by interpreting add 2 3 and, months later, generate code fast enough to train a language model.

## Week 0: prerequisites (C, memory, IRs, tensors, matmul, Python or OCaml)

- [C and pointers](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/01-c-and-pointers): Every compiler in this course ends by printing C. To read that C, you need one picture in your head: memory is a long row of numbered bytes, and a pointer is just one of those numbers.
- [Memory and caches](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/02-memory-and-caches): Two loops can do exactly the same arithmetic and differ in speed by ten times or more. The difference is the order they touch memory. From week 6 on, your grade depends on getting that order right.
- [Compilers and IRs](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/03-compilers-and-irs): A compiler is a program that reads a program and writes a different program that means the same thing. In the middle it holds the program as a data structure called an IR. This course is about...
- [Tensors are a buffer plus a way to read it](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/04-tensors-and-shapes): A tensor looks like a grid, but memory is a single row of numbers. Shape and strides are the rule that turns a grid position into a spot in that row. Most of an ML compiler is moving that rule around...
- [Matrix multiply is a pile of dot products](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/05-matmul): You only need one piece of linear algebra for this course: the dot product, and matrix multiply as a grid of them. Most of the compute in a neural network is matrix multiply, so most of the speed...
- [OCaml crash course](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/06-ocaml): You're going to write your compiler in OCaml. This is the subset of the language you need to start, taught with examples that have nothing to do with compilers, so that every line of compiler code is...
- [Python for this course](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week0/07-python): You're going to write your compiler in Python. You probably know the language already. This lesson is about the parts that matter for a compiler: a project the grader can run, the places where...

## Week 1: UOps and rewrites

- [The UOp: one node type for everything](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week1/01-the-uop): Your whole compiler is built from one tiny data structure: an op name, a tuple of source nodes, and an argument. Programs are graphs of these. This lesson is about why that's enough, and the trick...
- [The .uir format, and running it](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week1/02-uir-and-interpreting): .uir is the text form of a UOp graph: one node per line. Your first milestone is an interpreter (a program that runs another program directly instead of translating it). It reads the file, builds...
- [Rewrites and constant folding](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week1/03-rewrites-and-folding): A compiler pass is mostly a list of small rules like add(x, 0) → x, applied over and over until none of them fire. This lesson shows how that loop works, one rule at a time.
- [Symbolic simplification](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week1/04-symbolic): Constant folding needs every input to be known. Symbolic simplification works on values you don't know yet, like a param. It uses algebra and ranges to prove things like "this compare is always true".
- [call, param, stack and index](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week1/05-call-and-param): Week 1 programs can define functions. A function is just a graph with holes in it: param marks a hole, and call fills the holes and evaluates the graph.
- [The week 1 lab](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week1/06-lab): Build a compiler that parses .uir, type-checks it, runs it, and simplifies it. Write it in your own repo, in the language you picked in the sidebar. You're done when every week 1 test passes and...

## Week 2: memory and rendering C

- [Buffers and views](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week2/01-buffers-and-views): Week 1 programs computed values from constants and call arguments. Real kernels read and write memory that lives outside the program: model weights, activations, the output you hand back. This week...
- [Load, store, after](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week2/02-load-store-after): A store changes memory, but a graph has no "now". This lesson shows how .uir says when a write happens without any statement order: every store makes a new version of the buffer, and every load names...
- [Proving bounds](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week2/03-bounds): The syllabus says loads and stores are "bounds checked to never be out of range". Our compiler doesn't check at run time. It proves, before anything runs, that every view is inside its memory, using...
- [Rendering C](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week2/04-rendering-c): Rendering turns a graph into straight-line C: put the nodes in an order the memory rules allow, give every value a name, and print each one as a C statement that means exactly what the .uir op means...
- [The runtime](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week2/05-the-runtime): Rendering gives you C source. A runtime turns that source into answers: write it to a file next to a generated main, compile it, run the program, and read the buffers back out of its output, bit for...
- [The week 2 lab](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week2/06-lab): Extend your week 1 compiler with memory: buffers, views, loads, stores, and versions, checked for order and bounds. Then teach it to print C. You're done when every week 2 test passes, week 1 still...

## Week 3: loops

- [Ranges and ends](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week3/01-ranges): Week 2 programs touch every element by hand: one view, one store, one after per element. That's fine for four elements and hopeless for a thousand. This lesson adds the two ops that make a loop...
- [Memory in loops](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week3/02-memory-in-loops): A loop body runs again and again over the same storage. Week 2's rule, that every load names the version it reads, still holds, but "the version" now changes every iteration. This lesson covers the...
- [A GEMM by hand](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week3/03-gemm): The syllabus says that with loops "we can write gemms and convs in this language". This lesson writes the GEMM: C = A @ B on flat row-major buffers, three nested ranges, and one accumulator per...
- [Convolutions](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week3/04-conv): A convolution slides a small kernel along an input and takes a dot product at every position. With range and end you can write one by hand: two loops for a 1D convolution, four for a 2D one. The only...
- [Rendering loops](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week3/05-rendering-loops): A program with ranges is still a graph: nothing in it says "this line goes inside that loop". Your renderer has to work that out. Every value gets a depth from the ranges it depends on, every end...
- [The week 3 lab](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week3/06-lab): Add loops to your compiler: range and end in the type checker, loop-carried memory in the interpreter, and nested for loops in the renderer. You're done when every week 3 test passes, weeks 1 and 2...

## Week 4: rangeify, reduce, materialization

- [Vectors](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week4/01-vectors): Until now every ALU op took scalars, and to touch many elements you wrote a loop by hand. This week values get a shape again: an ALU op can take two vectors and combine them element by element. Your...
- [Reduce and expand](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week4/02-reduce-expand): Elementwise ops keep a vector a vector. Two more ops change shape: reduce collapses a vector to one number, and expand stretches one number into a vector. Between them they cover sums, means, maxima...
- [Rangeify](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week4/03-rangeify): The syllabus puts it in one line: "rangeify removes shapes from all ops." Your run can evaluate vectors directly, but your render can't unroll a 4096-element vector into 4096 lines of C. It has to...
- [Fuse or materialize](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week4/04-materialization): The syllabus says it plainly: "We have to confront questions about materialization here." Rangeify answers "what is your element at index i?" one loop at a time. When a value is used in two loops, it...
- [Rendering vectors](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week4/05-rendering-vectors): After rangeify, your renderer is printing a week 3 program, so most of this lesson is about what the output should look like and how to check it. The short version: one loop per rank-1 store, one per...
- [The week 4 lab](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week4/06-lab): Teach your compiler to take whole-vector programs and turn them into loops itself: rank-1 ALU, reduce, expand and stage in the type checker and interpreter, and a rangeify pass in front of your week...

## Week 5: movement ops (reshape, permute, pad, shrink, any rank)

- [Any rank, flat memory](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/01-shapes): Until now every value was a scalar or a vector. From this week a value can have any number of axes: a matrix, a stack of matrices, a batch of images. Memory doesn't change at all. Buffers stay one...
- [Reshape and permute](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/02-reshape-permute): Both ops rearrange a tensor without computing anything. reshape keeps every number in its place and changes how you count. permute keeps the numbers and changes which axis is which. They look alike...
- [Pad, shrink, expand, stack](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/03-pad-shrink-expand): Four more ways to rearrange without computing: grow a tensor with zeros, cut a window out of it, repeat it along a size-1 axis, or join several into one. With these, lesson 5.2's two, and index from...
- [Matmul and conv from movement](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/04-matmul-conv): A matrix multiply is a few movement ops, one mul and one reduce. So is a convolution. Once your compiler handles movement ops, it can express the two operations that do almost all the work in a...
- [Rangeify movement ops](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/05-rangeify-movement): Movement ops never compute anything, so rangeify can make them disappear. Each one becomes a little index arithmetic in front of a load: a multiply, a divide, a clamp. After rangeify, a matmul...
- [The week 5 lab](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/06-lab): Lift the rank limit. Your type checker learns shapes of any rank and the four movement ops, run evaluates them, and your rangeify pass turns each one into index arithmetic. You're done when every...

## Resources

- [Debugging your compiler](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/debugging): A red test is information. This page is the routine: read what the grader says, find out what the test is for, shrink it until the bug has nowhere to hide, and compare with the oracle.
- [Glossary](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/glossary): Every term the course uses, in plain words, with the lessons that teach it. Search below, or jump to a letter.
- [When you're stuck, or curious](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/): The lessons teach each idea once. These pages are for the second pass: reviewing before a lab, finding out why a test fails, looking up a word, or going further than the course does.
- [Python and OCaml, deeper](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/languages): The lessons teach enough of your language to build each week's compiler. This page is the next layer: the idioms and design patterns that make that compiler easier to write, the traps each language...
- [Quiz review](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/review): Every quiz from a week on one page. Answer them again before the lab, or bring back only the ones you didn't get right the first time.
- [Week 1 test guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/tests-week1): A test failed and you don't know why? Find it here: what it checks, and the plausible bugs that are known to fail it. Then read the matching part of the week 1 spec.
- [Week 2 test guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/tests-week2): A test failed and you don't know why? Find it here: what it checks, and the plausible bugs that are known to fail it. Then read the matching part of the week 2 spec.
- [Week 3 test guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/tests-week3): A test failed and you don't know why? Find it here: what it checks, and the plausible bugs that are known to fail it. Then read the matching part of the week 3 spec.
- [Week 4 test guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/tests-week4): A test failed and you don't know why? Find it here: what it checks, and the plausible bugs that are known to fail it. Then read the matching part of the week 4 spec.
- [Week 5 test guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/tests-week5): A test failed and you don't know why? Find it here: what it checks, and the plausible bugs that are known to fail it. Then read the matching part of the week 5 spec.
- [Week 0 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week0): Week 0 is the toolbox: C and memory, what an IR is, tensors as views of flat memory, matrix multiply, and enough Python or OCaml to write a compiler. Use this page to review before week 1, or to find...
- [Week 1 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week1): Week 1 builds the core everything else stands on: the hash-consed UOp, a type checker, an interpreter, and a rewrite engine that simplifies programs. This page recaps it, collects the rules worth...
- [Week 2 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week2): Week 2 adds memory and turns your compiler into one that prints C. The ideas are few but strict: memory comes in versions, every access has to be provably in range, and the C you print must have no...
- [Week 3 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week3): Week 3 adds loops. A range is a loop counter, an end repeats an effect for every value of it, and your compiler learns to place each value at the right loop depth and print for loops. This page...
- [Week 4 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week4): Week 4 lets you write whole-vector programs: elementwise ops on rank-1 values, reduce, expand and stage. Your compiler turns them back into week 3 loops by itself, a pass called rangeify. This page...
- [Week 5 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week5): Week 5 lifts the rank limit. Values can have any rank while memory stays flat, and four movement ops (reshape, permute, pad, shrink) rearrange them without computing anything. A matmul or a...
